project_scope.note: Local Malvoideae-first learner now uses multiple REAL installed species from Malvaviscus, Callirhoe and Abutilon (and Sida for habit variation), not Turk's cap alone. Broad Malvaceae includes relatives for which a projecting staminal column or winecup epicalyx is not universally typical.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: START at the actual flower: most local mallows have FIVE PETALS and numerous stamens joined into one STAMINAL COLUMN with many anthers, surrounding the styles. Then inspect the five-part CALYX, any extra ring of small BRACTLETS below it (EPICALYX/INVOLUCEL), paired STIPULES at foliage leaf bases and the mature FRUIT. Many have alternately arranged palmately veined leaves. Never use the presence of an epicalyx as a whole-family rule.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Commonly alternate/spiral and stipulate; palmate venation and stellate hairs are frequent supporting characters.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Local mallow-subfamily flowers commonly have five petals, a five-part sepal CALYX and many stamens fused by their FILAMENTS into a central STAMINAL COLUMN (monadelphous). An additional involucel/EPICALYX is variable among genera and even named Callirhoe species. Sources conflict about whether Williamson County Callirhoe pedata bears 3 bracteoles; the photo lesson must not claim certainty until botanists reconcile this.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Several local mallows (Callirhoe and Abutilon) mature a dry segmented SCHIZOCARP with separate MERICARPS (individual wedge-like fruit sections). Malvaviscus commonly makes a fleshy red segmented fruit. Hibiscus may produce a capsule. Mature fruit separates superficially similar flower forms.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Before counting petals: locate a small STAMINAL COLUMN with multiple anthers. CALYX = green flower sepals; EPICALYX/INVOLUCEL = an EXTRA ring of bractlets below that calyx; STIPULES = two appendages at a LEAF BASE along the stem. Those are THREE different anatomical landmarks. True fruit photos are needed to count MERICARPS.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: flower center and staminal column → open versus furled petals → palmately lobed leaves and habit → calyx versus epicalyx concept → dry schizocarp fruit and mericarps → genus variation → specialist diagnostic macro gaps
visual_lesson.intro: A mallow does NOT have to look like a hibiscus. See a Turk's cap flower with curled petals, an open winecup, a small yellow Abutilon blossom and dry fruit, and a small Sida plant—then identify shared structures: five petals, the fused staminal COLUMN, a true CALYX, any extra BRACTLETS beneath it (EPICALYX), STIPULES along the stem and fruits made of MERICARPS.

steps.title: 1 · Flower center: many stamens, one central column
steps.photo_role: fused staminal column / exserted floral center example
steps.look_for: In Turk's cap, the LONG projection beyond the folded red petals includes the fused staminal COLUMN and STYLES. The little pollen-bearing ANTHERS belong to many individual stamens united around that column. The flower is not a red tube with a solitary stamen.
steps.why_it_matters: A fused group of many stamens is a powerful local mallow-family (Malvoideae) clue versus families with separate stamens.

steps.title: 2 · Five open petals can make a winecup
steps.look_for: Count the FIVE MAGENTA PETALS radiating around the pale flower center. Contrast an OPEN winecup with Turk's cap, whose five petals remain tightly furled. Both belong to the mallow family.
steps.why_it_matters: Teaching the same floral plan in radically different shapes prevents reliance on flower silhouette.

steps.title: 3 · Spreading stems and palmately lobed leaves
steps.look_for: Trace the winecup stems spreading across the ground and leaves divided into PALMATE lobes (segments spreading outward from a central point). The whole plant shows a trailing perennial habit, not a species-defining flower color.
steps.why_it_matters: Growth form and foliage provide important supporting evidence when several local mallows have similar-colored blooms.

steps.title: 4 · Turn the winecup sideways and hunt for the epicalyx
steps.look_for: This Callirhoe pedata picture provides FLOWER and BUD context, not proof of the critical bractlets. To teach the EPICALYX, request a verified close-up of C. involucrata (e.g. UT Austin PlantPics exterior epicalyx view); compare the extra bractlets BELOW the true calyx with the actual calyx lobes. Note FNA vs UT conflicting pedata descriptions.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates calyx (sepals) from epicalyx (bractlets), and demonstrates why a blurry flower view cannot settle a microscopic character.

steps.title: 5 · Look at mallow leaves and developing fruit together
steps.look_for: Find the lobed leaves and fruit-bearing shoots on the winecup plant. A true mature MERICARP (one dry section of a many-parted mallow fruit) is not verified at dissection scale by this view.
steps.why_it_matters: Introduces the transition from flower to dry segmented fruit without pretending a general habit photo provides precise ripe fruit detail.

steps.title: 6 · Different flower color, same mallow staminal design
steps.look_for: Texas Indian mallow has FIVE YELLOW PETALS, not wine-purple. At the center is a cluster of anthers supported by the joined STAMINAL COLUMN; observe the contrast to Callirhoe while recognizing the same family pattern.
steps.why_it_matters: Flower color is not a reliable family or genus separator; floral parts are what matter.

steps.title: 7 · Dry segmented fruit: Abutilon example
steps.look_for: The Abutilon fruit is a compact circle of MERICARPS (individual fruit sections). Compare this dry fruit with the fleshy fruit expected in Turk's cap, and note that capsule-producing relatives exist. This is an Abutilon example, NOT a Callirhoe fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Gives a real photographed fruit example to connect the mallow flower with its mature reproductive architecture.

steps.title: 8 · A small-flowered mallow can look very different
steps.look_for: Spiny sida is a small-flowered mallow with toothed leaves; its overall habit looks nothing like winecups or Turk's cap. Its small diagnostic spiny tubercles beneath leaf petioles require a detail macro rather than being assumed from the whole-plant photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows family breadth and why leaves/flowers/fruit need to be combined for field identification.

steps.title: 9 · Specialist photo: involucel vs calyx side by side
steps.look_for: A future pair should show C. involucrata's separate small BRACTLETS beneath its five true CALYX lobes, with a verified second species at the same scale. The conflicting published C. pedata bractlet description must be explicitly resolved before a negative comparison is asserted.
steps.why_it_matters: Reliable species identification requires proving the precise flower architecture, not just memorizing bractlet terminology.

steps.title: 10 · Specialist photo: ripe fruit and stellate hairs
steps.look_for: Need an enlarged true ripe Callirhoe MERICARP and an independently verified star-shaped STELLATE hair photo, plus the paired STIPULES at a leaf base. None of the eight installed lesson examples guarantees these tiny features in detail.
steps.why_it_matters: Adds stronger fruit and leaf-surface evidence for comparing mallows with poppies, spurges and rockroses.

comparisons.title: Malvaceae vs Papaveraceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have many stamens. Local mallows commonly fuse them into a staminal column; prickly poppies have numerous free stamens and a capsule.

comparisons.title: Winecup versus Texas Indian mallow
comparisons.rule: Both show five petals and central fused stamens; Callirhoe involucrata has showy magenta winecup flowers and a trailing habit, whereas Abutilon fruticosum has small yellow flowers and compact dry schizocarp fruit. Use fruit/calyx, not flower color alone.

comparisons.title: Epicalyx vs calyx vs stipules
comparisons.rule: Epicalyx = extra BRACTLETS immediately below flower's CALYX; calyx = actual SEPALS enclosing petals in bud; stipules = paired appendages at base of ordinary LEAVES on a stem. C. involucrata has verified epicalyx, while whether C. pedata has bracteoles is disputed between FNA and a UT Williamson County botanical description.

comparisons.title: Mallow column versus papaver/poppy free stamens
comparisons.rule: A fused STAMINAL COLUMN supports many anthers in many local mallow subfamily flowers. Argemone and many rockroses display numerous separate FREE stamens; check staminal anatomy and fruit, not merely a five-petaled cup.

visual_lesson.caveat: The broad modern Malvaceae includes lineages more diverse than the five-petaled local Malvoideae examples. Some local genera have no epicalyx; Callirhoe involucrata's bractlets cannot be treated as a whole-family feature. A Calyx/epicalyx closeup remains required. Published FNA and UT Williamson descriptions of C. pedata conflict about bractlets; no conclusive arrow or negative character is asserted in these installed photo cards.
visual_lesson.photo_coverage_note: Eight real physically installed licensed species photographs anchor the lesson (Malvaviscus one, Callirhoe involucrata three, C. pedata one, Abutilon two, Sida one); two macro-only steps clearly unanchored. Callirhoe digitata/leiocarpa current website-referenced pictures are external/copyright-controlled and NOT counted installed.

family_confusion_cleanup.look_here_first: In local Malvoideae inspect the central staminal column with many anthers around the style; then calyx/epicalyx, stipules, and mature fruit. The column is not universal across broad Malvaceae.

comparisons.difference: Usually free stamens rather than a fused staminal column; compare flower centers and capsule versus mallow mericarps.
Argemone has free stamens and a syncarpous capsule; many local mallows have a staminal column and segmented fruit.
Geranium and Erodium have free stamens and conspicuously beaked schizocarps.
Stellate hairs alone do not decide family; compare unisexual flowers and often three-part capsules against mallow floral column and mericarps.

exceptions: Epicalyx variable; Callirhoe leiocarpa is an important no-epicalyx comparison.
Malvaviscus has fleshy fruit unlike dry mericarps of Callirhoe, Abutilon and Sida.
Fused staminal column is a local Malvoideae cue, not universal Malvaceae.
genus_routing: Malvaviscus: furled petals, exserted staminal column, fleshy fruit.
Callirhoe: check epicalyx and dry mericarps.
Abutilon: count style branches and inspect mericarp tips; use existing genus comparison.
Sida: small flowers, dry mericarps and calyx.
Sphaeralcea: stellate foliage and mallow flower; use fruit rather than color.
